CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-scans-only approach for automatically detecting and outlining tumors

The results show that commenting does not contribute to misinformation dissemination if users can distinguish true and false information, but does so if they cannot. 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer's research demonstrated a direct connection between these equivalent classes and the group Sp_n(K) itself. He achieved this by developing a method of associating a hermitian form with each conjugacy class and showed that these forms are equivalent across the class. Furthermore, he established a fundamental theorem that defines the hermitian form as a collection of equivalence classes, where the equivalence relation is determined by the existence of an element within the group Sp_n(K) that can transform one form into another. This thesis significantly builds upon previous work by Dieudonné and Demazure, with a notable emphasis on the characteristics of the field K. It also delves into the characteristics of the group Sp_n(K) itself, exposing its internal structure. The translation of Springer's thesis maintains the original format and formatting of his written work, ensuring a seamless reading experience for those interested in the historical development of mathematics within this specific context

While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. Our results show that our approach yields superior performance, as measured by classification accuracy, on a wide range of datasets, encompassing both real-world datasets and specially designed synthetic datasets, without requiring an excessively large number of features. Our novel method has the added benefit of allowing the user to influence the quality of the approximation through the selection of a parameter that is easily interpretable and directly related to the underlying data. We make the raw data used in our experiments, as well as the implementation of our method, freely available for the benefit of the machine learning community. We further extend the scope of our work by applying our method to the specific task of image classification, obtaining a notable improvement in classification accuracy

Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By computing this value for all single-node removals during an attack without immunization, as well as for the corresponding randomized model, the micro-level approach is demonstrated to be an effective way to assess network vulnerability. The results obtained from real networks and standardized random models align with theoretical predictions and provide valuable insights into network vulnerability, revealing that networks have areas of high vulnerability that cannot be predicted by broad measures. These areas correspond to the connections between the largest component and the isolated nodes that could join the main component and spread disease or malicious information. The micro-level approach can be used to evaluate the efficacy of network immunization and the effectiveness of strategies to prevent the spread of diseases or malicious information in networks. The algorithmic complexity of this micro-level approach is the same as traditional methods, but the computational cost is significantly lower, making it a useful tool for large networks. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as the average transmission rate. In this research, we develop a method to calculate the average transmission rate under both permanent and intermittent super-spreader influences. When a permanent super-spreader exists within the community, we derive an adjusted average transmission rate that considers the impact of the super-spreader's behavior and network connections. When super-spreader events occur intermittently, we employ renewal theory to determine the average transmission rate, taking into account the effects of these events on the transmission dynamics. We further observe that the effectiveness of our method diminishes when the frequency of these events becomes excessively low, as this scenario is characterized by an extended period without a super-spreader event, during which the transmission rate may rise above an unstable equilibrium, leading to widespread infection. This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. 
ReCross's effectiveness is demonstrated across nine different tasks from five datasets, along with reduced performance gaps when compared to supervised settings. 
The proposed method's versatility is also showcased by applying it to a task that requires both few-shot classification and dense sentence embedding generation. 
The code for ReCross has been made publicly available. 
With only a minor increase in computation, our method achieves notable improvements, paving the way for widespread adoption of efficient, unsupervised cross-task generalization in vast language models. 
Conversely, using ReCross at scale, as exemplified by using 100k samples, can be achieved with a manageable budget equivalent to fine-tuning a model for 1-5 epochs. 
This study's key findings highlight the potential of unsupervised retrieval to enhance the robustness of massive models in the face of new, unrelated tasks.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are currently attributed to the "remote epitaxy" category, where atomic layer deposition on graphene appears to grow films on the underlying substrate instead of the graphene surface. In this study, we investigate the effects of varying graphene orientation on lamellar bulk Al2O3 thickness, employing X-ray diffraction as our primary measurement tool. Our findings contradict our initial assumptions and reveal a surface-specific epitaxial process, where the film surface area is minimized to facilitate growth, rather than the lattice match between the graphene and the deposited material. We successfully modulate the film's surface area by altering the graphene lattice through heating treatments and methane exposure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that precise control over the graphene surface can result in scalable, smooth Al2O3 thickness through the deliberate creation of grain boundaries in the graphene substrate. We show that a particular type of grain boundary, where two triangular lattices meet, can lead to an approximate 3 times decrease in the Al2O3 thickness, likely due to an approximate 3 times increase in the film's surface area as it accommodates the larger surface energy of the triangular graphene lattice. We believe this study provides a fundamental understanding of the atomic layer deposition process on graphene and suggests that precise control over the graphene surface will be crucial for realizing the remote epitaxy

We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. Within the framework of Kay's covariant quantum algebras, this relationship also implies a form of implementation of time-translation symmetry. Ultimately, this work offers a formal, state-dependent version of Haag's theorem, which holds for specific types of quantum systems. We further explore the notion that the abstract adjoint relationship embodies a kind of quantum reciprocity, capturing a form of mutual relationship between observables and states that defines the essence of physical consistency. We examine the implications of defining the abstract adjoint relationship for particular types of states, such as pure phases or equilibrium states. We also explore its connection to the concept of topological order as an emergent property of covariant algebras that arise from specific types of ground states. We propose that the abstract adjoint relationship provides the foundation for a renewed approach to quantum field theory that focuses on states rather than algebras, offering a means to study the intricate relationships between different ground states

smartphones, fitbits, and vehicular sensors has led to an explosion in data generated through daily activities.  As a result, researchers and practitioners are increasingly drawn to machine learning methods for various applications.  These initiatives typically call for large-scale data sets to be used for training purposes.  Unfortunately, implementing such a strategy in everyday scenarios is often infeasible due to the limited amount of high-quality data available.  In real-world settings, datasets are frequently marred by issues such as poor data quality, limited quantity, and lack of relevance.  Such challenges are particularly pronounced in inception tests, where collecting suitable data is extremely difficult given the long history required.  For instance, gathering data from daily activities would be insufficient as it would not capture rare events from the user's life.  Conversely, gathering large quantities of data from everyday life on a particular behavior would be impossible as it would necessitate the behavior occurring frequently enough to go undetected by the user.  In the context of the MNIST digit dataset, a similar paradox could be formed with digits the user knows, where digits the user does not know would again require frequent usage to go undetected.  To resolve this issue, we propose a novel machine learning approach called "steep learning" that enables effective model training even with minimal, low-quality data.  The method, which is applicable to various machine learning algorithms, reduces reliance on large data sets by leveraging a unique combination of constraints that steer the model's focus

It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the problem aims to determine the minimum
required transmission count, denoted as N, to accurately decode the original transmitted
sequence.
We have previously established a lower bound for this problem as (d-r+N-1)/2 + 1
for sequences of the binary alphabet and provided a achievable transmission count of
(d-r+1)/2 + 1 for sequences of the binary alphabet with a fixed code.
In this research, we broaden the applicable domain from binary to alphabet of size
q and demonstrate that a achievable transmission count for an arbitrary alphabet
equates the previously established lower bound. Hence, we can conclude that in the
binary domain, the achievable and lower bounds for the sequence reconstruction
problem coincide. Moreover, we achieve this equality without any restriction on
the code used in the transmission process. It is worth noting that previously used
proof techniques are not applicable in the larger alphabet domain. We utilize a
novel approach based on the Gray code induction method.

In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning, which enables robust performance even in the presence of substantial, unpredictable changes. We examine the sources of uncertainty in the models themselves, in their training procedures, and in their applications, and investigate how these uncertainties affect continual learning. Building upon this concept, we propose the "Einstein Experiment" utilizing a versatile, table-top setup based on a double-Slit setup with a variable slit configuration, allowing for both passive measurement of quantum properties and active detection of a single particle. By adapting this setup from demonstration of quantum non-locality and counterfactual quantum bit storage to the Einstein Experiment, we demonstrate the feasibility of achieving the same results using a setup that either measures quantum properties directly or detects a single particle at a specific location, showing that such a setup yields the same quantum state as required by the Einstein Experiment. This document presents the novel FL-V2X framework, a federated learning environment tailored for V2X applications, incorporating real-time 5G communications and V2X data simulations. AR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. These changes included shortening the antenna and closing a feedback loop to stabilize the helicon mode. With these modifications, the source was able to achieve significantly higher plasma densities, hot electron content, and particle power conversion, all at lower magnetic fields. These results demonstrate the potential of the IShTAR source to effectively interact with radio frequency waves, which will be crucial for achieving the necessary plasma interaction in future civil fusion devices.
